summary:
Earth’s changing surface leaves clues, but satellite radar can be difficult to discover and interpret. SARFlow — See Earth Move turns that complexity into an accessible journey: Explore → Understand → Investigate.

We developed an interactive web platform and Android preview that help users discover NASA–ISRO NISAR observations, explore geographic locations, compare dated radar visualizations, and follow the evidence behind each view. A beginner-friendly learning experience explains radar concepts, while a Numerical Analysis Lab demonstrates change calculations using clearly labeled synthetic data. A separate real GCOV reader check demonstrates access to calibrated radar measurements.

SARFlow connects discovery, visualization, education, and provenance without hiding scientific uncertainty. It helps students, educators, and curious explorers move from “What am I seeing?” to “What evidence supports my interpretation?” Our goal is to make Earth observation easier to explore and harder to misunderstand.
details:
SARFlow
Earth’s surface is constantly changing. The difficult part is turning satellite observations into questions people can investigate responsibly.

SARFlow — See Earth Move is an interactive Earth-observation platform developed by SPACE BUDDIES for Dancing with the SARs. It helps users discover NASA–ISRO NISAR observations, understand radar imagery, compare observations across dates, and inspect the sources and limitations behind an investigation.

Our central idea is simple: a beginner should be able to explore satellite radar without confusing an attractive visualization with a scientific conclusion.

Explore → Understand → Investigate

Users begin with a place. World Explorer provides interactive geographic navigation, place search, coordinate entry, map zoom, and contextual basemaps. Global Radar Explorer connects locations to available NISAR catalogue records and dated browse imagery, helping users investigate what observations are available.

The Place Observatory brings observations into a shared geographic workspace. Users can inspect acquisition dates, switch between observations, compare imagery with swipe and opacity controls, and play through discrete acquisitions. The prepared regional archive covers the Brahmaputra floodplain, Puget Sound, Sacramento Valley, and Rasuwa, Nepal. Playback advances through actual available dates; it does not generate intermediate ground motion.

The learning experience explains why radar images differ from ordinary photographs. A beginner guide, learner video, and scientific explanations introduce active microwave sensing, backscatter, polarization, product types, and interpretation limits. Optical basemaps provide geographic context and remain separate from radar measurements.

The Numerical Analysis Lab makes the calculation process visible. Using explicitly labeled synthetic teaching arrays, it demonstrates common-valid pixel support, optional averaging in linear power, logarithmic power change, adjustable thresholds, histograms, and threshold sensitivity. These examples help users understand the method without presenting simulated results as measured environmental change.

Follow the evidence

SARFlow connects the visual experience to available source records. Users can inspect acquisition information, product identifiers, imagery requests, processing settings, and scientific limitations. Available evidence exports preserve the relevant context so an investigation can be examined beyond the screen.

The project also includes a separate real NISAR Level 2 GCOV reader check. An Arctic acquisition was read using documented quality-support rules, retaining 4,096 supported pixels in each HH and HV channel within a 64 × 64 diagnostic window. This demonstrates access to real calibrated numerical observations. It does not establish a before-and-after environmental event or independent scientific validation.

The bundled project resources include 15 archived NASA GIBS visualization scenes, six archived NASA CMR metadata records, four prepared regions, three synthetic teaching cases, and one verified single-acquisition GCOV reader check. These categories describe different resources and are not combined into a single dataset total. On-demand discovery may expose additional observations.

How we built it

The interface uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and MapLibre GL JS. A Node.js/Express backend coordinates observation discovery, location search, and imagery-related requests. NASA CMR and ASF services support catalogue discovery, while NASA GIBS supplies radar browse visualizations. Python modules use tools including NumPy, h5py, Rasterio, and PyProj for GCOV reading and experimental geospatial processing.

The responsive website supports desktop and mobile browsers. The installed Android preview provides access to the hosted application through a WebView, with browser handoff for relevant external actions. It is an online preview, and we do not claim that it contains an independently implemented native analysis engine.

Creativity and intended impact

SARFlow’s creative contribution is the connection between geographic curiosity, interactive learning, observation comparison, and traceable evidence. Users can move from a global map to a dated observation, from a visual difference to a methodological question, and from that question to its supporting sources.

Students can learn radar concepts through interactive examples. Educators can demonstrate how satellite investigations work. Researchers and Earth-observation enthusiasts can discover observations and inspect their provenance. The intended impact is greater access to Earth-observation knowledge and better understanding of what satellite evidence can—and cannot—support.

Scientific responsibility and next steps

We considered accessibility, responsive interaction, source attribution, reproducibility, processing support, and uncertainty throughout the project. Catalogue metadata, browse imagery, synthetic calculations, calibrated measurements, and evaluated results are kept distinct.

Water analysis remains experimental. We have not completed an independently evaluated multitemporal NISAR flood investigation, and SARFlow is not an operational emergency-warning service. A visible radar difference is not automatically proof of flooding, damage, or displacement.

Our next priority is one reproducible Water & Wetlands investigation using compatible calibrated acquisitions, documented quality masks, appropriate reference observations, and independent evaluation. We would connect the resulting layers and evaluation evidence to the investigation interface before expanding to additional domains.

SARFlow’s ambition is to make the journey from curiosity to evidence accessible: Explore Earth. Understand radar. Investigate change.
